newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's trade surplus up in February.
newsitem.headline: Japan's trade surplus up in February.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus rose in February for the second consecutive month, the government said Monday, contributing to mounting U.S. concern over trade imbalances.

Tokyo's surplus in its current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose 15.4 percent to 865.2 billion yen ($6.92 billion) in February from a year earlier, the Ministry of Finance said.
The surplus was slightly above economists' average forecast of 801.1 billion yen ($6.40 billion) and followed a rise in January, the first in 17 months.
Japan's surplus in merchandise trade alone rose 2.9 percent to 878.0 billion yen ($7.02 billion) from the same month a year earlier.

The current account data was closely watched by financial markets following last Friday's visit to Tokyo by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who urged Japanese officials to guard against a resurgence in the trade surplus.
A further rise in Japan's current account surplus would re-ignite trade friction with Japan, Rubin said.
But Monday's news of a widening of the surplus failed to dent bullish sentiment toward the dollar, which jumped to a 50-month high of 125 yen.
Currency dealers said the alarming tone of Rubin's comments on the surplus was offset by his vow not to use currencies as a trade tool, which emboldened dealers to continue buying dollars.
"We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else," Rubin said on Friday.
Dealers said they took the remark to mean that Washington still wanted a strong dollar. The U.S. currency has steadily risen since hitting a post-war low just under 80 yen two years ago.
Economists said the surplus was likely to continue rising, with current account data showing that Japan's economic growth owed a great deal to strong exports.
"(It provides) good evidence that Japanese exports benefit from the gain in competitiveness, as well as a pick-up in global demand," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at J.P. Morgan.

Although Koll said he did not expect the surplus to trigger a shift in trade policies in either the United States or Japan, he expected Tokyo's current account surplus to expand from 1.5 percent of the nation's gross domestic product to 2 percent by the end of this year.
Economists generally believed, however, that a sustained resurgence in Japan's surplus may open the door for a change in U.S. policy.
Rubin also pointed out that there was great interest around the world in what additional strategies Japan might pursue if the surplus keeps rising.
Japanese officials have so far reacted coolly to the surplus' recent rise, acknowledging only that the pace of the broader year-and-a-half-long decline was slowing.
They also maintained that structural changes, such as a shift overseas of Japanese manufacturing, continued to support import growth.
